title: Narration Mock Test

questions.solution:
He said that he was reading a book. is correct.
Present continuous → Past continuous; "I" → "he"

She told me that she had finished her work. is correct.
"said to me" → "told me"; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "my" → "her"

They said that they would go to Delhi the next day. is correct.
"will" → "would"; "tomorrow" → "the next day"

He told her that she was very intelligent. is correct.
"said to her" → "told her"; "you" → "she"; Present → Past

My mother said that she had cooked dinner the night before. is correct.
Simple past → Past perfect; "last night" → "the night before"

The teacher told the students that the earth revolves around the sun. is correct.
Universal truth — tense does NOT change; "said to" → "told"

She said that she had been watching TV when he had called. is correct.
Past continuous → Past perfect continuous; Simple past → Past perfect

He said that he could speak three languages. is correct.
"can" → "could" in reported speech

She told me that she would be waiting for me. is correct.
"shall" → "would"; future continuous stays as would + be + V-ing; "you" → "me"

He said that he had to leave then. is correct.
"must" (obligation) → "had to"; "now" → "then"

She said that she might come to my party. is correct.
"may" → "might" in reported speech

He told us that he had been working there for five years. is correct.
"said to us" → "told us"; Present Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous; "here" → "there"

The doctor said that that medicine should be taken twice a day. is correct.
"should" does not change; "this" → "that"

She said that she had never visited Shimla before the month before. is correct.
Past Perfect stays Past Perfect; "last month" → "the month before"

He told me that he would have completed the project by Friday. is correct.
Future Perfect "will have" → "would have"; "Friday" is specific — no change needed

My friend said that he had bought that pen the day before. is correct.
Simple past → Past perfect; "this" → "that"; "yesterday" → "the day before"

She said that she had not been feeling well when she had missed the class. is correct.
Both clauses shift: past continuous → past perfect continuous; past → past perfect

Both (A) and (B) are correct. is correct.
"need not" → "needn't" or "did not need to"; both are acceptable in formal grammar

She said that she had been waiting since morning. is correct.
Present Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous; "since morning" keeps "since"

He said that he used to play cricket when he was young. is correct.
"used to" is a past habit — stays unchanged in reported speech

The principal told the staff that they should submit their reports by the following Monday. is correct.
"said to" → "told"; "you" → "they"; "your" → "their"; "Monday" → "the following Monday"

She said that neither of them was coming that day. is correct.
Present continuous → Past continuous; "today" → "that day"; "is" → "was" (singular subject)

He said that he had already eaten dinner when she arrived. is correct.
Past Perfect stays; Past simple stays if it follows past perfect — both clauses already in the past

She told me that she could not help me that time. is correct.
"cannot" → "could not"; "this time" → "that time"; "you" → "me"

The reporter told that the minister was attending the conference at that time. is correct.
Present continuous → Past continuous; "said" has no object so "told" needs object — (C) is correct phrasing

He said that he would be free the following afternoon. is correct.
"will" → "would"; "tomorrow afternoon" → "the following afternoon"

She said that she had just posted the letter. is correct.
Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "just" is retained

The officer told the clerk that he had been absent without notice the day before. is correct.
Past simple → Past perfect; "you" → "he"; "yesterday" → "the day before"

He said that he might have misunderstood me. is correct.
"may have" → "might have"; "you" → "me"; no object for "said" so (A) is standard

She said that she was born in that city twenty years before. is correct.
Birth — factual/historical event: tense stays as simple past; "this" → "that"; "ago" → "before"

She asked me if I liked coffee. is correct.
Yes/No question → "if/whether" + assertive; "do" removed; "like" → "liked"; "you" → "I"

He asked her where she was going. is correct.
Wh-question: "where" retained; inversion removed (she was going); "said to" → "asked"

The teacher asked the students if they had finished the assignment. is correct.
Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "you" → "they"; "if" introduces yes/no question

She asked him when he had returned from abroad. is correct.
Simple past → Past perfect in reported question; no inversion; wh-word "when" retained

He asked me whether I was coming to the party that night. is correct.
"tonight" → "that night"; "are coming" → "was coming"; yes/no → "whether"

She asked her friend how long she had been waiting. is correct.
Present Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous; no inversion

He asked who had broken the window. is correct.
"who" as subject — no change in word order; Simple past → Past perfect

The manager asked the employee why he had been late that day. is correct.
Past simple → Past Perfect; "today" → "that day"; no inversion in reported question

She asked me whether I would help her with that task. is correct.
"will" → "would"; "this" → "that"; "me" (speaker) → "her"; yes/no question → "whether"

He asked her whether she had passed the examination. is correct.
Simple past → Past perfect; "Did she pass" → "whether she had passed"

She asked him what time the train arrived. is correct.
Present simple → Past simple; no inversion; "does" dropped

He asked me if I had ever been to Paris. is correct.
Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "ever" retained; "Have you" → "if I had"

The interviewer asked the candidate what motivated him. is correct.
Present simple → Past simple; "you" → "him"; no "that" with wh-word

She asked him whether that was the book he had recommended. is correct.
"this" → "that"; "Is" → "was"; "recommended" → "had recommended" (past sequence)

He asked her if she could speak French. is correct.
"Can" → "could"; yes/no question → "if"; no inversion in reported question

She asked who was responsible for that mess. is correct.
"is" → "was"; "this" → "that"; no inversion; no "that" after wh-word

He asked me which route I had taken the previous day. is correct.
Simple past → Past perfect; "yesterday" → "the previous day"; no inversion

She asked her son if he had brushed his teeth. is correct.
Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "you" → "he"; "your" → "his"; yes/no → "if"

He asked which of them had broken the vase. is correct.
"you" → "them"; Simple past → Past perfect; "which" — no inversion

She asked him why he hadn't informed her earlier. is correct.
"didn't inform" → "hadn't informed" (Past → Past Perfect); "me" → "her"; no inversion

He asked me if I knew where she lived. is correct.
Double reported: outer "do you know" → "if I knew"; inner "where she lives" → "where she lived"

She asked her friend whether she was still in touch with Priya. is correct.
"Are you" → "whether she was"; "still" stays; no inversion

He asked what had made me so restless that day. is correct.
"has made" → "had made"; "today" → "that day"; "you" → "me"

The customs officer asked the traveller where he had come from. is correct.
"have come" → "had come"; "you" → "he"; wh-word before subject-verb

She asked him whose laptop that was. is correct.
"Whose" retained; "is" → "was"; "this" → "that"; no "that" after wh-word

He asked her how many times she had visited that place. is correct.
Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "you" → "she"; "this" → "that"; no inversion

Both (A) and (C) are correct. is correct.
Both forms are valid; the inner clause "was involved" may stay or shift to "had been involved"

Both (A) and (B) are correct. is correct.
Negative question in direct becomes "if/whether I did not want" — both (A) and (B) are correct

The judge asked the accused whether he had been present at the scene of the crime. is correct.
"Were you" → "whether he had been"; Past → Past Perfect; no "that" with yes/no

She asked him how much the painting had cost. is correct.
Simple past → Past perfect; wh-word "how much" kept; no inversion; "said to" → "asked"

She requested him to help her with the luggage. is correct.
"Please" = polite request → "requested him to"; no "please" in reported form

The officer ordered the soldier to stand at ease. is correct.
Military command → "ordered"; "Stand" → "to stand"

Mother warned the child not to touch that hot stove. is correct.
Negative imperative with safety = "warned not to"; (D) is also acceptable but (C) is more precise

He requested me to lend him my pen. is correct.
Tag with imperative = polite request → "requested" + infinitive

The doctor advised the patient to take that medicine three times a day. is correct.
Medical instruction = "advised"; "this" → "that"

She advised him never to tell a lie. is correct.
"Never + imperative" = strong moral advice → "advised him never to + V"

Both (B) and (C) are correct. is correct.
"Let us" = suggestion: can be "proposed that they should" or "suggested going/that they go"

The captain ordered the crew to man the lifeboats immediately. is correct.
Urgent command → "ordered"; "immediately" may be retained or changed to "at once" — (B) standard

She requested her friend not to tell anyone about that. is correct.
Negative request with "please" → "requested not to"; "this" → "that"

The judge ordered the witness to speak the truth and nothing but the truth. is correct.
Court command by judge = "ordered"

He ordered that there should be no noise in the hall. is correct.
"Let there be" (3rd person let) = command/order; appropriate reporting verb = "ordered"

Both (B) and (C) are correct. is correct.
Conditional imperative: both "told...if" or "advised to... and would" forms are valid

The coach advised the player not to let pressure get to him. is correct.
Coaching advice = "advised"; "you" → "him"

He exclaimed joyfully that they had won the match. is correct.
"Hurrah!" = exclamation of joy: "exclaimed joyfully/with joy that"; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "we" → "they"

She exclaimed sadly that her favourite vase was broken. is correct.
"Alas!" = exclamation of grief: "exclaimed sadly/with sorrow that"; "my" → "her"; "is" → "was"

He exclaimed admiringly that it was a very beautiful painting. is correct.
"What a...!" = exclamation of admiration → "exclaimed admiringly/with admiration that + it was + very + adj + noun"

She exclaimed that he was very clever. is correct.
"How + adj!" → "exclaimed that + subject + was very + adj"; "you" → "he"

All of the above are acceptable reported forms. is correct.
"Bravo!" = applause/admiration; multiple valid reporting expressions exist

Both (A) and (C) are correct. is correct.
Optative sentence with "May" = wish/prayer: "prayed/wished that might" — both are correct

She wished she could turn back the clock. is correct.
"If only" = strong wish → "wished that/she + could"; no "if only" in reported form

He ordered them to shut up and sit down. is correct.
Rude command → "ordered"; (D) may be used contextually but "ordered" is grammatically standard

She told the peon to get her a cup of tea. is correct.
Instruction to subordinate = "told"; "me" → "her"

He permitted him to do whatever he wanted. is correct.
"Let + 3rd person" = granting permission: "permitted/allowed him to"; "wants" → "wanted"

She requested him not to be late for the interview. is correct.
"Please + negative" = request; "said to" → "requested"; proper infinitive form: "not to be"

The general ordered his troops to advance and capture the enemy position. is correct.
Military command = "ordered"; (D) "commanded" also acceptable, but standard exam answer = "ordered"

Both (A) and (C) are correct. is correct.
"What a pity!" = exclamation of sorrow/regret; "missed" → "had missed"

Both (A) and (B) are correct. is correct.
National/ceremonial wish = "prayed that might" or "wished that would" — both valid

She told him to make himself at home. is correct.
Hospitable instruction = "told"; "yourself" → "himself"

He warned them to beware of the dog. is correct.
Warning = "warned"; subject needed: "them"; infinitive: "to beware of the dog"

Both (B) and (C) are correct. is correct.
Exclamation of anger + indirect question element; multiple valid reported forms

She told him that she had been thinking about what he had said the day before. is correct.
Present Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous; "yesterday" → "the day before"; both clauses shift

He told the interviewer that he was confident that he could handle the pressure. is correct.
"said to" → "told"; both "am/can" → "was/could" in reported speech

She said that she would have helped me if she had known about it. is correct.
Third conditional (hypothetical past) — both parts stay unchanged; "you" → "me"

He expressed that he wished he were a millionaire. is correct.
Subjunctive "were" stays; "wish" (present reporting verb sense) → no further tense shift needed for the wish

The scientist said that water boils at 100°C at sea level. is correct.
Scientific truth — tense is NEVER changed in reported speech

She told him that she would never forget the day they first met. is correct.
"shall" (1st person) → "would"; "we first met" → "they had first met" (past in reported clause)

He said that he had been told that the project had already been cancelled. is correct.
"was told" → "had been told" (passive past → passive past perfect); inner clause stays

She told me that she might not be able to attend unless I rescheduled. is correct.
"may" → "might"; "unless you reschedule" → "unless I rescheduled"; pronoun shift "you" → "I"

He said that he would rather stay home than go to the party. is correct.
"would rather" = modal expression stays unchanged in reported speech

Both (A) and (C) are correct. is correct.
Both maintain the meaning; dropping "that was" and using participial phrase is stylistically acceptable

He said that he had barely fallen asleep when the phone had rung. is correct.
Both clauses already past: first → stays Past Perfect; second past simple can → past perfect as sequential

She told him that unless he apologised, she would not forgive him. is correct.
Conditional: "apologise" → "apologised"; "will" → "would"; "you" → "him"; "I" → "she"

The chairman said that they had achieved a record profit that year. is correct.
"said" with no object; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; "this year" → "that year"; "we" → "they"

He told her that he had been meaning to talk to her about something important. is correct.
Present Perfect Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous; "you" → "her"

She said that no sooner had she entered the room than the lights had gone out. is correct.
"No sooner did" → "no sooner had...than" with past perfect; both clauses shift to past perfect

Both (A) and (B) are correct. is correct.
"must" (urgency/necessity) can become "must" or "had to"; "will" → "would"; both valid

She said that she would appreciate it if he could be a little more considerate. is correct.
Polite conditional with "would/could" — no tense shift needed; "you" → "he"

He said that neither had he seen such courage nor would he ever forget it. is correct.
Correlative conjunction preserved; "have" → "had"; "will" → "would"; inversion preserved in reported subordinate

She told him that even if he tried his best, he might not succeed. is correct.
"try" → "tried"; "may" → "might"; "you" → "he"; "said to" → "told"

Both (B) and (C) are correct. is correct.
"dare not" (semi-modal) → "dared not" or "did not dare to" — both are grammatically correct

She told him that he looked pale and asked whether he had been feeling unwell lately. is correct.
Two sentences: assertive + interrogative; "look" → "looked"; "Have you been" → "had been"; "lately" stays

He said that he wondered whether she would come or not. is correct.
"wonder" (thinking aloud) → "wondered"; "will" → "would"; "whether...or not" retained

She told the audience that she would like to thank each and every one of them for their support. is correct.
"you" → "them"; "your" → "their"; "would like" stays (polite form); "said to" → "told"

He apologised to her for what had happened the day before and promised that it would not happen again. is correct.
"I am sorry" → "apologised"; "yesterday" → "the day before"; "won't" → "would not"; "I promise" → "promised"

All of the above are correct reported forms. is correct.
Third conditional with inversion: all three variants are grammatically valid reported forms

He told her that he couldn't thank her enough for everything she had done. is correct.
"can't" → "couldn't"; "you've done" → "she had done"; "said to" → "told"

She said that the more she thought about it, the less certain she became. is correct.
Double comparative structure: both verbs shift — "think" → "thought"; "become" → "became"

He told his colleague that he had completed the analysis he had asked for. is correct.
"you" (the colleague) → "he"; "asked" → "had asked"; "said to" → "told"

She said that she had been under the impression that he had already left. is correct.
"was" → "had been" (past simple → past perfect for the outer clause); inner past perfect stays

He told the committee that he strongly believed that the decision should be reconsidered. is correct.
"believe" → "believed"; "should" stays (advisory modal); "said to" → "told"

He asked her why she had not replied to his message. is correct.
Simple past negative → Past perfect negative; "my" → "his"; "you" → "she"; no inversion

She said to me, "I have been working on the report since morning." is correct.
Past Perfect Continuous in indirect → Present Perfect Continuous in direct; "since morning" stays

The professor told the students to submit their projects by the following Friday. is correct.
"submit" = instruction → "told...to"; "your" → "their"; "next Friday" → "the following Friday"

He asked me if I did not think I should apologise. is correct.
Negative question softened to neutral indirect form; "you" → "I"; "think" → "thought"

She congratulated him on his promotion. is correct.
Exclamatory congratulation → "congratulated him on his promotion"

She told him that she could not tell him how grateful she was. is correct.
"cannot" → "could not"; "am" → "was"; "I" → "she"; "you" → "him"

The manager said to the staff, "The meeting has been postponed indefinitely." is correct.
Past Perfect passive in indirect → Present Perfect passive in direct; "indefinitely" stays

He said that he would love to visit Japan someday. is correct.
"would love" stays (already past modal form); "someday" may be kept or changed to "some day" — (A) is standard

She told him that she had not heard from him in a long time and asked if he was alright. is correct.
Two sentences combined: declarative + interrogative; tense shifts; "in a long time" stays

She suggested that they should not discuss that in public. is correct.
"Let's not" = suggestion → "suggested that they should not"; "this" → "that"

She said to me, "Why were you so silent throughout the meeting?" is correct.
Past Perfect in indirect → Simple Past in direct; "I" → "you"; "me" → her addressee

Both (A) and (B) are correct. is correct.
Optative "May you" = blessing/wish: "wished her a long life" or "prayed that she might live long"

He told her that he supposed she had not met his brother yet. is correct.
"suppose" → "supposed"; "haven't met" → "had not met"; "my" → "his"; "you" → "she"

She said that she wished she had taken that job when she had the chance. is correct.
"wish" (subjunctive) + past perfect: "said that she wished she had taken"; no further tense shift in wish clause

The station master announced that the train was to leave at 8 AM the next morning. is correct.
Scheduled/timetabled future: "leaves" can → "was to leave" or "would leave"; "tomorrow" → "the next morning" — (D) is the most precise SSC answer

He said that he would sooner die than betray his country. is correct.
"would sooner...than" = strong preference stays as is in reported speech; no tense change

She requested the manager to check if her application had been processed. is correct.
Polite request with "Could you please" → "requested to check"; "has been" → "had been"; no "please" in indirect

She exclaimed with interest that it would be interesting if they could travel back in time. is correct.
"How interesting!" = exclamation → "exclaimed...that it would be interesting"; conditional stays; "we" → "they"

He said that he was not the sort of person who gave up easily. is correct.
"am" → "was"; "gives" → "gave" (relative clause verb also shifts with the main verb)

The doctor told the patient that it was high time he started taking his health seriously. is correct.
"It's high time" + past subjunctive stays; "you" → "he"; "your" → "his"; "is" → "was"

She told him that she hoped he didn't mind her asking. is correct.
"hope" → "hoped"; "don't mind" → "didn't mind"; "my asking" → "her asking"

She said that she had hardly sat down when the doorbell had rung. is correct.
"Hardly had I" → "she had hardly"; both clauses already past; simple past "rang" → past perfect "had rung"

The inspector said to the suspect, "Were you at home yesterday evening?" is correct.
Past Perfect in indirect → Simple Past in direct; "previous evening" → "yesterday evening"

He said that he took pride in the fact that he had never broken a promise. is correct.
"take" → "took"; "have never broken" → "had never broken"; "the fact that" retained

He said that whether he agreed or not, he intended to go ahead with his plan. is correct.
"you" (audience) → "they" (in reported context); "agree" → "agreed"; "I intend" → "he intended"; "my" → "his"

She told him that she was telling him that for his own good. is correct.
"this" → "that"; "your" → "his"; "I'm telling" → "she was telling"

He told her that he would have called her but he had lost his phone. is correct.
"would have called" stays; "lost" → "had lost" (past → past perfect for sequence); "my" → "his"

The coach told them that the early bird catches the worm. is correct.
Proverb — tense is NEVER changed in reported speech

She exclaimed disbelievingly that she couldn't believe he had been keeping that a secret for so long. is correct.
Exclamatory + complex: "can't" → "couldn't"; "you've been keeping" → "he had been keeping"; "this" → "that"

Both (A) and (B) are correct. is correct.
Third conditional with inversion: both "had he paid" (retained inversion) and "if he had paid" are valid; "now" → "then"
